message: 28F. It burns when I pee and I'm going a lot more often, started 2 days ago. No fever, no back pain. I'm not pregnant. I've had UTIs before.

basis.quote: It burns when I pee and I'm going a lot more often, started 2 days ago
basis.interpretation: Current dysuria and urinary frequency for 2 days consistent with lower urinary tract infection; symptom onset is recent and progressive
Absence of fever and flank/back pain argues against pyelonephritis or upper tract infection on current report
Prior UTI history increases pretest probability of recurrent infection and may inform empiric treatment eligibility and follow-up monitoring

output.reason: Time-sensitive need for clinician assessment to confirm UTI diagnosis, prescribe antimicrobial therapy, and ensure appropriate follow-up.

output.reason: A 28-year-old with 2 days of dysuria and increased urinary frequency, denying fever, back pain and pregnancy, likely has uncomplicated cystitis needing clinician assessment and possible antibiotic prescribing, which can safely start in messaging.
output.patientMessage: Send this to a Counsel clinician in this thread today for assessment and possible antibiotic treatment; your burning and frequent urination fit a likely simple bladder infection. Meanwhile, drink fluids. If you develop fever, chills, back or side pain, vomiting, blood in urine, or symptoms worsen quickly, seek same-day in-person care regardless of whether a message reply has arrived.
differential: Urethritis from a sexually transmitted infection

redFlags.concern: Flank/back pain suggesting upper tract infection
Vomiting or inability to keep fluids down

output.vitalSigns: No vital sign values reported; whether temperature or other vitals were measured is unknown, though fever is denied by symptom report.
output.evidenceLimitations: Retrieved passages cover complicated UTI and other urologic emergencies, not outpatient management of uncomplicated cystitis in a nonpregnant adult.

citations.claim: Complicating factors such as pregnancy, obstruction, catheter, diabetes or immunosuppression drive escalation; none were reported here, supporting a routine outpatient pathway.
citations.limitation: ED reference synthesis listing complicating factors; absence of reported factors does not confirm absence.
